scope: Six preparation/procedure columns from reviewed clauses in the existing EPIT source fields. Two ion columns were derived separately from the reviewed v1 solution recipes. Old features, targets and composition were not changed.

policy.grit: Numeric reported grades were retained; mesh, slash and ambiguous emery notations were left unconverted. Abrasive particle size did not imply Ra.
policy.durations: Minutes/seconds were converted to hours. Bounds, different steps and post-pitting observation durations were not collapsed to one exact duration.
policy.method_combinations: The output listed distinct explicitly named operations, not inferred chronology. Earlier processing operations and final sample preparation were both retained when reported.
policy.preparation_solutions: Active chemical/electrochemical baths or explicitly named cleaning liquids; carrier/rinse water was not added to an active mixture. Different incompatible bath reports stayed unresolved.
policy.agitation: Explicit nonzero electrode rotation established 1. Gas bubbling, fixed electrode mounting and stationary current did not establish zero or one.
policy.outcomes: Only the listed procedure evidence clauses supplied features. No target, composition or outcome-dependent quantity was extracted.

The melt was cast in a purified argon atmosphere by drawing into 7mm dia. Vycor tubes and quenching in water. The alloys were homogenized at 1050°C for 17h, swaged to 0.4cm diameter rods, annealed at 1050°C and water quenched.

Heat treatment.source_text: The stainless steels evaluated in this study were prepared from commercially pure grades of Fe, Ni, ferrochrome, Mn, Mo, Si, manganese or chromium nitride, and chromium carbide. Melting was done in a vacuum induction furnace.The melting procedure consisted of: (1) melting Fe, Ni, Mo, Mn, and ferrochrome in a vacuum; (2) bleeding nitrogen into the furnace; and (3) introducing Mn4N or CrN, wrapped in iron foil, into the melt, as needed. After casting, only solid sections of the ingots were taken to prepare test specimens. The sections were first soaked for 30 minutes and hot rolled. The temperatures were 1205 C and 1095 C, depending upon hot ductility of the heats. The hot rolled specimens were pickled in a solution containing 10% HNO3 and 2% HF at 65 C to remove the hot working scale, cold rolled to 2 mm, annealed at 1065 C for 5 minutes, water quenched, and pickled again in the same HNO3-HF solution at 65 C. A small section was cut from each heat and used for chemical analysis.
evidence_clauses: pickled in a solution containing 10% HNO3 and 2% HF at 65 C
pickled again in the same HNO3-HF solution at 65 C
notes: The repeated pickling bath was identified as HF + HNO3. Percentage bases and pickling duration were not established. Heating/annealing durations did not become Prep_time, and bath temperature did not become CP_temp.

Heat treatment.source_text: The ingots were homogenized in A or He, usually at 1050-1100 oC for several hours. Ingots of Ni-Cr, Ni-Mo, and Cr-Fe were cold rolled to 0.25 cm, then annealed at 1000-1050 oC and water quenched. The Cr-Fe alloys containing more than 40% Cr were difficult to roll or swage, hence electrodes were machined directly from the homogenized ingot. Ingots of the lower % Cr-Fe alloys and of the stainless steels were swaged to about 0.45 cm diam rods, annealed at 1050 oC and water quenched. All electrodes measured approximately 2 cm long and were either 0.4 cm diam or 0.5 cm wide by 0.2 cm thick.

Heat treatment.source_text: Two sets of laboratory-prepared ferritic alloys and two commercial ferritic stainless steels (Types 430 and 4341) were investigated. The high-purity 17% chromium, 17% Cr-l% Mo, and 17% Cr-3% Mo laboratory alloys were prepared by melting and casting in vacuum. The resulting ingots were hot-rolled to 0.64-cmthick sheet, which was cold-rolled to a 0.32-cm thickness, annealed for 1 hr at 815~ and water-quenched. The 18% Cr-2% Mo alloys modified by titanium and Type 434 is the proposed designation for stainless steel conraining 17% chromium and 1% molybdenum. nickel additions were produced by induction melting in an argon atmosphere, using the split-heat technique. In this technique, the base composition is melted, and part of the melt is poured off to produce an ingot; then to the balance of the melt, the required alloying additions are made and the next ingot is cast. This process is repeated until a series of the desired compositions is cast. The 18% Cr-2% Mo ingots were hotforged, hot-rolled to 0.76-cm-thick strips, and coldrolled to 0.38-cm-thick strips. The 18% Cr-2% Mo alloys containing titanium were annealed for 1 hr at 104O~ the minimum temperature that prevented formation of a second phase in the high titanium alloy, and then water-quenched. The rest of the 18% Cr-2% Mo materials and the hot-rolled, commercial Types 430 and 434 steels were annealed at 815~ for 1 hr and water-quenched.
notes: No additional approved preparation feature was established by this description; existing environment/history fields were preserved.

Heat treatment.source_text: In this technique, the base composition is melted and part of the melt is cast into an ingot. To the balance of the melt, the required molybdenum addition is made and the next ingot is cast. This process is repeated until a series of the desired positions is cast. By this procedure, the residual and impurity elements, which were intended to be in the range commonly present in commercial stainless steels, were held essentially constant within each series. The ingots were hot-forged and hot-rolled to a thickness of 0.76 cm and then cold-rolled to 0.38 cm. The 13% nickel steels were annealed at 1120C for 1 hr and water-quenched. The 39% nickel steels and the high-purity alloys were annealed at 1150C for 1 hr and water-quenched.

Heat treatment.source_text: All surfaces of the cast slabs were ground to remove imperfections and provide good rolling surfaces before annealing 16 hours at 1200C in argon atmosphere. The slabs were hot rolled at 1090C to 1/16 inch thickness. Oxide scale was subsequently removed by sand blasting before a final annealing treatment. Following preparation, each alloy was hot rolled to 0.1 inch sheet and water quenched. Hot rolling temperatures were restricted to a maximum of 982C and a minimum of 816C. The hot rolled sheet was electropolished in an aqueous 15wt% NaCl/ 30wt%H2SO4 electrolyte to remove surface scale and sheared into 1 inch wide strips running parallel to the hot rolling direction. The 1 inch wide hot rolled strips were subsequently cold rolled from 0.1 inch to a final thickness of 0.0625inch.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Potentiodynamic Polarization with exposed area of 1 cm2. Potentiodynamic polarization experiments were carried out using a scan rate of 0.1 mV/s commencing at a potential about 250 mV more active than the stable OCP. Before starting the polarization scan, the specimen in the sample holder (WE) was left in the cell for about 1 h to attain a steady state which is shown by a constant potential and current at the beginning of the experiment. The potcntiodynamic runs were programmed such that upon attaining a current density of 25μA/cm^2, the scan direction was reversed and the potentials were scanned back to the starting potential.
evidence_clauses: Before starting the polarization scan
left in the cell for about 1 h
notes: About one hour was retained as the reported nominal pre-scan equilibration duration.

notes: No additional approved preparation feature was established by this description; existing environment/history fields were preserved.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Following pretreatment for 5 min at -1.5 V, the potential was increased-rapidly to -0.5V and thereafter at a steady rate of 1V in 50 min. In this work the critical pitting potential was taken as that at which there was an anodic current flow of 10^-5 A/cm^2.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Polarization curves were obtained potentiodynamically at a scan rate of 20 mV/min, using a Tacussel electrochemical set composed of a potentiostat, a current recorder, and a high impedance electronic millivoltmeter.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Potentiodynamic Polarization. The potential was controlled by a Wenkingt potentiostat (Model 68 TS-3) and changed in steps of 10 mV with a Wenking SMP 69 scanning potentiometer every hour for the positive polarization direction until the onset of pitting or appearance of pits, and every 100 s for the reverse scan until zero current. The potential was initially held at 150 mV for 1 h to attain stable current, whereupon the scanning potentiometer was activated.
evidence_clauses: initially held at 150 mV for 1 h to attain stable current
notes: The explicit initial potential hold supplied preparation duration. Later hour-long potential steps did not supply CP_time.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Potentiodynamic Polarization. For pitting tests, specimens were allowed to passivate in air for at least 18 h prior to testing.
evidence_clauses: passivate in air for at least 18 h
notes: Air passivation was retained as a preparation method. Its lower-bound air-exposure duration was not chemical/electrochemical Prep_time or test-bath CP_time.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Potentiodynamic Polarization. Potentiodynamic sweeps in hot 3.5% NaCl solution were carried out at a rate of 1 mV s-1. The tests were carried out in a glass three-electrode cell held in a water bath at 65 °C. In all experiments the rod under test was supported in a holder on the lid of the cell such that the end face just touched the surface of the test solution as described above. The counter electrode was a platinum wire, the reference electrode a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) at the same solution temperature; all potentials are given against the SCE. The potential at which the current density exceeded 50 uA cm-2 was defined as the pitting potential.
notes: No additional approved preparation feature was established by this description; existing environment/history fields were preserved.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Potentiodynamic Polarization. the sample was kept immersed in the experimental solution for 5 min at open-circuit potential (OCP). The anodic potential was increased in steps of 20 mVSCE, and the current readings were recorded after waiting at each set potential for 1 min.
evidence_clauses: immersed in the experimental solution for 5 min at open-circuit potential
notes: The five-minute initial open-circuit wait was retained; subsequent one-minute waits at each applied potential were measurement steps, not additional CP_time.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Potentiodynamic Polarization. All solutions used were deaerated with high-purity argon for at least 2 h before analysis. Potentials were measured against a saturated calomel electrode (SCE). Cathodic pretreatments were performed in 0.1 M hydrochloric acid (HCl) for 15 min at –700 mV SCE , while the current was monitored, in order to remove the air-formed oxide film.

notes: The preparation bath was HCl. The separate two-hour argon purge was not specimen equilibration time. No preparation concentration or redox column was added.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Potentiostatic Polarization, Potentiostatic polarization curves were obtained at 25°C and at 0°C in N,-saturated 0.1N NaCl and O*lN NaBr. The electrode totally immersed was first polarized in the least noble passive region for 15min, then the potential was moved in the noble direction 50mV every Smin until the pitting potential was approximated and the current showed a marked increase. This was followed by longer-time runs of 12-15h at a single potential in the neighbourhood of the critical potential in order to establish the steady state value. The least noble potential at which the current did not continuously increase with time and at which no pits could be observed under a low power microscope was taken as the final value.
evidence_clauses: first polarized in the least noble passive region for 15min
notes: The initial conditioning interval was 15 minutes. Later potential steps and 12-15 hour measurements were not preparation or equilibration durations.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Polarization test, strips of 1.25 cm x 1.25 cm of the experimental alloys, as well as the commercial alloys, were subjected to anodic polarization in dearated 1 N NaCI solution at 30 C. A Type 308 rod was welded to one side of each specimen and covered with rubber tubing, except the tip for electrical connection to a potentiostat. The specimens were then mounted in epoxy, ground to 600 grit, and rinsed with distilled water. The specimen/mount interface was covered with a thin film of lacquer, and approximately 1 cm 2 of the specimen was exposed. They were then kept in a desiccator until testing. The testing procedure consisted of: (1) introduction of the solution to a one liter polarization cell; (2) setting the temperature of the solution; (3) deoxygenating the solution with prepurified nitrogen at the rate of 90 ml/min starting 30 minutes before immersion of the specimen; (4) cleaning the specimen with distilled water just prior to transferring to the cel]; and (5) anodic polarization 50 minutes after the immersion at a scanning rate of 20 mV/min, using a PAR Model 173 potentiostat and ELSCINT Model ABA-26 Automatic Baseline Advance.
evidence_clauses: ground to 600 grit, and rinsed with distilled water
anodic polarization 50 minutes after the immersion
notes: 600 was retained as the reported grade, without asserting a grading standard. Fifty minutes of specimen immersion became 50/60 h; the separate 30-minute gas purge before immersion was not CP_time. Rinse water was not added to the active pickling bath described elsewhere.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Potentiodynamic Polarization, the specimen surface was ground to a 120 grit finish and 5 cm2 was exposed to the corrodent. [Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Potentiostatic Polarization. The experimental procedure was to first polarize the electrode potentiostatically at the least noble potential within the passive region for at least 15 min in order to achieve steady-state passivity. The potential was then advanced in stages of 50 mV, allowing 5 min between each change. Initially the current decreased or remained constant after each potential adjustment, but eventually a steadily increasing current at some potential V'c indicated the onset of pitting (or of transpassivity). Steady-state values Vc were obtained subsequently by holding the potential for long times at a fixed value and then observing pitting or the lack of it under a low power microscope. The lowest potential for which pitting could not be observed after a 10-hr or longer period of constant polarization was considered to be the steady-state value Vc. Reproducibility was in the order of ±5 mv.
evidence_clauses: first polarize the electrode potentiostatically
for at least 15 min in order to achieve steady-state passivity
notes: At least 15 minutes was a lower bound, not an exact preparation duration. Any different earlier pickling time was not substituted for this conditioning duration. Later 5-minute steps and >=10-hour pitting observations were excluded.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: Potentiodynamic Polarization. The onset of pitting was marked by a sharp and sudden increase in polarization current. The potential scanning was stopped at the pitting potential, and the electrode was allowed to pit for 20 to 30 min. It was then removed from the solution, the tape was stripped, and its surface was examined for pitting and possible crevice corrosion. The potential scanning was usually started at -0.7 to -0.6v, with respect to the saturated calomel electrode (SCE); the scanning was always into the passive potential region. In some experiments, the potential of an actively corroding electrode was changed almost instantaneously to a selected potential in a passive range by switching on a potentiostat, with a potential preset at a desired value.

[Cl-] Test Method.source_text: The "scratch" technique was employed for the determination of pitting potentials.The electrode was first polarized potentiostatically to some potential well below the expected pitting potential.The polarization current was allowedto stabilize and then the electrode surface was scratched with a sharp silicon-carbide crystal mounted on the end of a glass tube. The electrode potential was manually adjusted by 20 mV steps to more and more noble potential values, until the scratch failed to repassivate, a failure which was indicated by a gradual current rise after the electrode was scratched. The pit was allowed to develop for 10 min, and then the electrode was examined visually. Only those results were considered to be valid where pits actually developed at the scratched site.

Some small second-phase particles also occurred. Electron microprobe analysis identified these particles as carbides (Me23C6 type) and carbonitrides (Me23C6 type). Pure nitrides were very rare. Comments.source_text: In the as-received specimens of the 18Cr-5Ni-0.03Mn steel, metallographic examination revealed the presence of martensite with some inclusions of 𝛿-ferrite. As determined by X-ray analysis, the alloys with more than 5% Mn contained austenite and ferrite. No traces of 𝜎-phase were detected. The amount of 𝛿-phase depended upon the steel composition. The higher the Mn content was and the lower the C and the N contents were, the greater the amount of 𝛿-phase present. However, heat-to-heat variations also very likely influenced the phase composition of the alloys under investigation. In all specimens, small particles of a foreign phase were detected. They were identified by electron probe analysis as carbides (presumably Me23C6).

Comments.source_text: To prevent the initiation of crevice corrosion between the epoxy and specimen, the epoxy-specimen interface was painted with Amercoat 90 epoxy leaving an exposed area of 1 cm2 on the material surface. The painted sample was cured in an oven for 10 h at 70C. Just before introduction into the polarization cell, the exposed metal surface was polished by hand with cloth and a 9-microm diamond paste to remove the air-formed oxide film created during the epoxy curing process. The interface seal was abraded slightly but not damaged. Polarization tests were conducted in an aerated electrolyte.

Comments.source_text: Al Alloy, For most of the measurements, Al electrodes were employed measuring 1.5 cm long and 0.4 cm in diameter. One end of each electrode was drilled and tapped, allowing a threaded member attached to a nickel wire to hold the electrode firmly against a glass tube separated by a water-tight Teflon gasket. Only the electrode surface, totally immersed, Teflon, and glass made contact with the electrolyte. Specimens were polished to 3/0 emery paper followed by pickling in 2N NaOH at 80~ for 5 min and then washing in distilled water.
